anomaly_def.Name: Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk table and index pages have become physically or logically corrupt, so the storage structures no longer match the logical contents they are supposed to represent.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly : The physical storage layer cannot deliver the sustained read/write bandwidth, IOPS, or latency required by the database engine, causing prolonged I/O waits and stalled page and log traffic.

When both anomalies are present, the database exhibits a mixture of corruption-style and saturation-style symptoms: index and consistency checks intermittently fail while ordinary queries suffer unpredictable slowdowns; identical statements alternate between missing rows and hanging on I/O waits; recovery, backup, or CHECKDB-like operations may run for excessive durations and still report page, key-order, or checksum errors; log flush latency spikes co-occur with corruption detections, triggering repeated automatic page repairs, forced page flushes, or emergency readahead that further prolong I/O queues; monitoring shows rising wait times for both corruption-related retry logic and device-level bottlenecks, making it difficult to attribute the primary performance degradation.

The causal interplay stems from the fact that storage congestion increases the likelihood that partially written pages, torn writes, or incomplete index rebuilds persist long enough to escape detection, while corrupt blocks force the engine to perform extra physical reads, retries, and redundancy checks that inflate I/O volume and queue depth. Each corrupted page or index inconsistency often causes re-reads, repair attempts, or fallback full scans, all of which demand additional throughput from an already saturated storage subsystem. Conversely, sustained high queue depths and latency windows during peaks extend the vulnerability period for write interruptions (power loss, controller resets), thereby increasing the chance of structural corruption. Together, the two root causes form a feedback loop that amplifies both data-integrity risks and performance degradation, rapidly eroding overall database availability and reliability.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
